v: Understand that Hangul is built, not memorised

b.v: Korean is not written in pictures. It has an alphabet of 24 letters, invented in 1443 so that ordinary people could read. Letters are grouped into square blocks, one block per syllable. Learn the letters and you can read anything — even before you know what it means.

v: 아  a  — like the a in father
야  ya — like ya in yard
어  eo — like the o in son
여  yeo— like yu in yummy
오  o  — like the o in go
요  yo — like yo in yoga
우  u  — like oo in moon
으  eu — no English match; lips flat, like a short grunt
이  i  — like ee in see

b.v: 아 야 어 여 are the same shape with the stroke on the other side, or doubled. Notice the pattern and you halve the work.
A vowel cannot stand alone in writing. It needs a consonant in front. When there is no consonant sound, Korean writes ㅇ, which is silent in that position. That is why 'a' is written 아 and not ㅏ.

v: Write each vowel five times with ㅇ in front: 아 야 어 여 오 요 우 유 으 이
Say each one out loud as you write it
Cover the list and read them in a different order

b.v: Some letters have two sounds. ㄱ sounds closer to g between vowels and closer to k at the start or end of a word. Do not fight this — it settles by ear.
A syllable is written as a square. Consonant first, then vowel. Tall vowels go to the right, wide vowels go underneath.

v: ㄱ + ㅏ = 가 (ga) — tall vowel, sits to the right
ㄱ + ㅗ = 고 (go) — wide vowel, sits underneath
Build these yourself: ㄴ+ㅗ, ㅁ+ㅡ, ㅅ+ㅣ, ㅂ+ㅏ
Understand why Korean has levels of politeness

b.v: 1) The greeting you will use most

v: 안녕하세요 = annyeonghaseyo = hello (polite, any time of day)
안녕 = annyeong = hi / bye (only with close friends or children)

b.v: 안녕하세요 works morning, afternoon and night. Korean has no separate 'good morning' for strangers.

v: 안녕히 계세요 = annyeonghi gyeseyo = goodbye, said to the person staying
안녕히 가세요 = annyeonghi gaseyo = goodbye, said to the person leaving

b.v: If you are walking out of a shop you say 안녕히 계세요 (annyeonghi gyeseyo, "stay well") to the shopkeeper, because they are the one staying. They say 안녕히 가세요 (annyeonghi gaseyo, "go well") to you, because you are the one leaving.

v: 감사합니다 = gamsahamnida = thank you (formal, safe everywhere)

b.v: Korean changes the verb ending depending on who you are speaking to. Using the casual form with a stranger or an older person sounds rude, not friendly. As a learner, stay with the 요 ending and you will never offend anyone.

v: Greet three imaginary people out loud
Leave a shop: say 안녕히 계세요
Ask the same of someone else

b.v: Korean puts the topic first and the verb last. 'I am Khalid' comes out as 'I-as-for Khalid am'.

v: 저는 칼리드입니다 = jeoneun Khalid-imnida = I am Khalid
저는 파키스탄에서 왔어요 = I came from Pakistan

b.v: Notice 국 (guk) at the end of several country names. It means 'country'.

v: 이름이 뭐예요? = ireumi mwoyeyo? = what is your name?
어느 나라에서 왔어요? = eoneu naraeseo wasseoyo? = which country are you from?
만나서 반갑습니다 = mannaseo bangapseumnida = pleased to meet you

b.v: Say the whole thing out loud, replacing the name and country with your own:

v: 안녕하세요. 저는 ___입니다. 파키스탄에서 왔어요. 만나서 반갑습니다.
Count in both Korean number systems
Know which one to use when

b.v: About 30 minutes. This is the day that surprises most learners.
1) Korean has two sets of numbers
One is native Korean, one is borrowed from Chinese. They are not interchangeable. Which one you use depends on what you are counting.
2) Sino-Korean — for money, dates, minutes, phone numbers
Above ten you just stack them: 11 is 십일 (ten-one), 20 is 이십 (two-ten), 35 is 삼십오.
3) Native Korean — for counting things, age, hours

v: Money, dates, minutes, phone numbers, floors → Sino-Korean
Things you can point at, your age, the hour → native Korean
Time mixes both: 3:20 is 세 시 이십 분 — native for the hour, Sino for the minutes

b.v: Do not try to learn both perfectly today. Learn 1–10 in both and let usage teach you the rest.

v: Count to ten twice, once in each set
Say your age in native Korean + 살 (sal)
Read a price out loud in Sino-Korean
Say what you like and cannot eat

b.v: 2) Dishes you will see on any menu

v: 비빔밥 bibimbap = rice with vegetables and egg, mixed
불고기 bulgogi = sweet marinated grilled beef
김밥 gimbap = rice and fillings rolled in seaweed
떡볶이 tteokbokki = rice cakes in spicy sauce
이거 주세요 = igeo juseyo = this one, please
메뉴 주세요 = menyu juseyo = menu, please
물 주세요 = mul juseyo = water, please
얼마예요? = eolmayeyo? = how much is it?
계산서 주세요 = gyesanseo juseyo = the bill, please

b.v: 주세요 (juseyo) means 'please give me'. Put any noun in front of it and you can order almost anything.

v: 돈지고기 안 먹어요 = I do not eat pork
매운 거 못 먹어요 = I cannot eat spicy things

b.v: Order a meal out loud: greeting, menu, one dish, water, the bill.

v: Use the words for here, there and over there
저기 jeogi = over there, away from both of us
화장실이 어디예요? = where is the toilet?
역이 어디예요? = where is the station?

b.v: 쪽 (jjok) means 'side'. 오른쪽 is literally 'right side'.

v: Ask for the toilet, the station and a pharmacy
Answer yourself: 오른쪽에 있어요 = it is on the right

day-8.t: Day 8 — Verbs and the 요 ending

b.v: About 30 minutes. This is the most useful lesson in the course.
In the dictionary, every Korean verb ends in 다 (da). That is the plain form. You never say it that way in conversation — you cut off 다 and add an ending.

v: 가다 gada = to go → 가요 gayo = I go / you go / we go
먹다 meokda = to eat → 먹어요 meogeoyo
보다 boda = to see → 봐요 bwayo

b.v: 2) The 요 ending does a lot of work
Korean does not change the verb for I, you, he or she. 가요 can mean I go, you go, he goes, they go. Who is doing it comes from the context, or you say it once at the start.

v: Put 안 (an) in front: 안 가요 = I do not go
안 먹어요 = I do not eat
안 봐요 = I do not watch

b.v: Say the same sentence with a rising tone. Nothing else changes.

v: Turn all ten verbs into the 요 form
Ask three of them as questions
Say the days of the week

b.v: Every day ends in 요일 (yoil). Only the first syllable changes.
Remember Day 5: native numbers for the hour, Sino numbers for the minutes.

v: 몇 시예요? = myeot siyeyo? = what time is it?
이거 주세요 = I will take this one
카드 돼요? = kadeu dwaeyo? = do you take card?
Say what day it is today
Ask the price of three things
Hold a short conversation start to finish
Review everything from the first nine days

b.v: Read this out loud twice, then cover the English.

v: B: 안녕하세요. 이름이 뭐예요? — Hello. What is your name?
A: 저는 칼리드입니다. 파키스탄에서 왔어요. — I am Khalid. I came from Pakistan.
B: 만나서 반갑습니다. — Pleased to meet you.
A: 실례합니다, 화장실이 어디예요? — Excuse me, where is the toilet?
B: 오른쪽에 있어요. — It is on the right.
B: 안녕히 가세요. — Goodbye (to the one leaving).
Read any Korean word, even without knowing it
The subject markers 이 / 가 and how they differ from 은 / 는
Counting words — Korean uses a different one for people, animals and flat things
Listening: Korean drama with Korean subtitles, not English ones

b.v: The single best thing you can do now is read Hangul out loud every day, even signs you do not understand. Reading speed comes before everything else.
Record yourself saying the whole conversation above. Play it back. That is your baseline — come back in a month and record it again.
